title: Retrieval-Augmented Knowledge Platform for Regulated, Multi-Tenant Documentation
summary: A multi-tenant retrieval platform that answers questions against controlled documentation, with tenant-scoped permissions enforced at query time and every answer traced back to the passages it quotes.
role: Sole engineer, from schema design through deployment
team: Solo, with one subject-matter reviewer for the corpus

cover.alt: Placeholder standing in for the project cover image.

overview: The platform sits between a controlled documentation corpus and the people who have to act on it. Each tenant brings its own documents, its own classification rules, and its own idea of who may read what, and the system has to answer questions without ever assembling one tenant's answer out of another tenant's text.

Retrieval is hybrid. A lexical index catches the exact terms, identifiers, and clause numbers that embeddings routinely blur, a vector index catches paraphrase, and the two ranked lists are fused before a cross-encoder reranks whatever survives. The answer is composed only from the passages that made it through, so every sentence has something to point at.

The parts that took longest were not the model-facing ones. Permission propagation, re-ingesting a changed corpus without taking search offline, and making a wrong answer legible enough to debug are what the architecture is actually shaped around.
capabilities: Answers natural-language questions against a per-tenant documentation corpus
Enforces tenant and role scoping inside the index rather than after the ranking
Fuses lexical and vector retrieval, then reranks what survives
Cites the exact passage behind every sentence it produces
Declines to answer when nothing clears the relevance floor
Re-ingests a changed corpus incrementally, without taking search offline
Traces a query end to end, from request through to the passage set it used
Replays a fixed evaluation set against every build and reports what changed

features.title: Permission-aware retrieval
features.body: Tenant and role filters are pushed into the index and enforced again by row-level security in the database. Filtering a ranked list after the fact still tells a reader that documents they cannot open exist, which is a subtler failure than showing them the text.

features.title: Hybrid search with rank fusion
features.body: Lexical and vector results are merged by rank rather than by score, because the two scales were never comparable and normalising them invents a relationship that is not there. Fusion by position is cheap and does not drift when either index is retuned.

features.title: Citations as a hard requirement
features.body: Composition is constrained to the passages that survived reranking, and each sentence carries the passage it came from. A sentence with no source is a bug in the composer, not a stylistic choice.

features.title: An explicit refusal path
features.body: When nothing clears the relevance floor the system says so and stops. A confident answer assembled from weak passages is worse than no answer, because it costs the reader the time it takes to find out it was wrong.

features.title: Incremental corpus ingestion
features.body: Documents are chunked, embedded, and indexed by a scheduled job with a forbidden concurrency policy, so a slow document delays the next run instead of overlapping with it. Search stays available throughout.

features.title: Tracing that reaches the passage set
features.body: One trace covers the request, both retrieval calls, the fusion, the rerank, and the composition, and carries the identifiers of the passages that were used. Debugging a bad answer starts from the trace rather than from a reproduction attempt.

features.title: A replayable evaluation harness
features.body: A fixed question set with known-good passages runs against every build and reports which questions changed answer. It is a regression signal rather than a score to optimise, and it is deliberately small enough to read in full.

features.title: Infrastructure described in one place
features.body: The database, the indexes, the object store, and the worker that fronts them are declared as Terraform, so a second environment is a variable file rather than an afternoon of console work.

codeSnippets.title: Ingestion as a scheduled job
codeSnippets.code:
# Ingest runs as a job, not inside a request. A document that takes ninety seconds
# to chunk and embed must not be able to hold a connection open while it does.
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: corpus-ingest
spec:
  schedule: "17 * * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never
          containers:
            - name: ingest
              image: registry.internal/knowledge/ingest:2026.08
              args: ["--source", "s3://corpus/incoming", "--batch-size", "64"]
              env:
                - name: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT
                  value: http://collector.observability:4317

lessons: Push authorisation into the index. A filter applied after ranking still tells a reader that something they cannot see exists.
Rank fusion beats score normalisation. Two scales that were never comparable do not become comparable by being rescaled.
An answer without a citation is not a shorter answer, it is a different product. Requiring one changed what the composer was allowed to do.
Refusing to answer needs to be a designed path with its own copy, not an empty state that fell out of a null check.
An evaluation set is worth more when it is small enough to read than when it is large enough to average.

caseStudy.challenge: Every tenant's corpus carried its own classification scheme, and the first working version applied those rules after retrieval. That was quick to build and quietly wrong: a filtered-out result still shifted the ranking of everything around it, and the shape of an answer told a reader that documents existed which they had no right to know about.
caseStudy.decision: Move the boundary down. Tenant and role scoping became arguments to the index query and a row-level security policy in the database, so the application cannot forget them and a mistake is one policy in one place rather than a missing condition at any of a dozen call sites. The cost is that retrieval and authorisation are now coupled: a permission change means running the query again, not re-filtering a cached list.
caseStudy.outcome: Results became reproducible per role, which is what finally made the evaluation harness mean something. The same question asked by two roles is now two comparable runs rather than one run and a filter. The coupling has held up; the part still unfinished is invalidating cached answers when a permission changes.
